It is essential to characterise fiber orientation in LFAM 
because the mechanical performance of the final part 
depends heavily on this internal microstructure. Traditional 
approaches involve imaging techniques such as scanning 
electron microscopy (SEM), followed by analysis of 2D 
cross-sections using ellipse fitting to estimate fiber orienta­

average alignment of fibers within a volume [1]. However, 
these methods are time-consuming and sensitive to opera­
tor bias. They also typically require multiple orthogonal 
sections for reliable tensor estimation [2]. High-resolution 
image acquisition is critical to ensuring the accuracy and 
repeatability of these measurements [3].
1  Introduction
Large Format Additive Manufacturing (LFAM) is an 
extrusion-based process used to manufacture large, custom 
composite parts for the aerospace, automotive and energy 
sectors. The primary advantage of LFAM is its ability to 
process thermoplastic materials reinforced with short fibers 
(typically 100–500µm in length) embedded in a thermo­
plastic matrix, enabling a combination of high throughput 
and enhanced mechanical properties. When fiber-reinforced 
thermoplastics such as acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS)

Abstract
Large Format Additive Manufacturing (LFAM) enables the rapid production of composite components using short fiber-
reinforced thermoplastics. This process offers high strength-to-weight ratios and efficient material deposition. However, 
the mechanical performance of printed parts is strongly dependent on fiber orientation. Reliable characterisation of ori­
entation remains challenging due to the limitations of manual microscopy analysis. It is further hindered by the scarcity 
of large, annotated datasets required for deep learning inference (i.e., the automatic prediction of fiber orientation from 
image data using trained neural networks). This study addresses this gap by proposing a physics-informed methodology 
for the synthetic generation of microscopy-like images that replicate the microstructure of LFAM-processed composites. 
The simulation pipeline, implemented in Python, creates large-scale datasets by generating non-overlapping ellipsoidal 
fiber distributions with known geometrical and statistical parameters. Each synthetic image is paired with an analytically 
computed orientation tensor. This enables the supervised training of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) without the 
need for manual annotation. The system allows full control over fiber orientation, aspect ratio, and area fraction. It is 
calibrated using real micrographs obtained via X-ray Microscopy (XRM). The resulting synthetic images closely repro­
duce the statistical features of real microstructures and provide robust ground truth for model training and validation. 
Overall, this scalable approach enables rapid dataset generation and facilitates the development of accurate AI models for 
automated orientation analysis. It also supports future applications in digital twin frameworks, in-line quality control, and 
material characterisation in LFAM.

Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have 
made it possible to automate image-based material charac­
terisation tasks. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) 
in particular have demonstrated significant potential for 
inferring fiber orientation from microscopy images [4] on 
CNN-based orientation prediction. However, training such 
models requires vast amounts of accurately labelled data. 
Manually annotating fiber orientations in micrographs is 
labour-intensive and prone to inconsistencies, rendering the 
use of experimental datasets alone impractical.
To address this challenge, the generation of synthetic 
data has emerged as a robust alternative. Python-based 
physics-informed routines can simulate realistic SEM-like 
images populated with fiber-shaped ellipses. Each image is 
generated using known fiber geometries and orientations, 
enabling the analytical computation of orientation tensors. 
This approach enables the creation of large, fully labelled 
datasets suitable for supervised deep learning. Synthetic 
datasets generated with controlled parameters ensure con­
sistency and overcome annotation uncertainty, making them 
ideal for robust AI training [5].
The basis of the current work is a custom Python-based 
algorithm that generates synthetic images replicating the 
fiber architecture observed in composites produced using 
LFAM. This simulation pipeline considers realistic geomet­
ric constraints such as aspect ratio, spatial distribution and 
non-overlap conditions, using parameters extracted from 
experimental datasets obtained through X-ray microscopy 
(XRM). Unlike traditional SEM, XRM enables virtual slic­
ing through the sample volume, yielding thousands of cross-
sectional images without causing any physical destruction. 
These virtual slices provide a solid basis for validating the 
fidelity of synthetic data and the performance of AI models.
Generative AI techniques, such as GANs [6] and VAEs 
[7], have shown promise for synthetic image generation in 
various fields. However, in the context of fiber-reinforced 
composites, these models often suffer from limitations such 
as mode collapse and lack of interpretability, which hin­
der their applicability in engineering scenarios that require 
traceability and parameter control. Recent reviews [8] for 
critical reviews of synthetic data strategies. In this regard, 
physics-informed simulations offer a deterministic and con­
trollable alternative, allowing direct access to ground-truth 
orientation tensors without the need for manual annotation. 
This aligns with our methodology, which uses an ellipse-
based model calibrated from experimental data to generate 
balanced, statistically realistic datasets suitable for super­
vised learning.
The proposed synthetic data generation system supports 
industrial workflows by enabling the training and validation 
of AI models that can automatically analyse fibre orienta­
tion [9, 10]. Once trained, such models can be deployed in 
real manufacturing environments where image-based qual­
ity control is required. The system can be integrated into 
digital twin frameworks (integration of trained CNN mod­
els into virtual replicas of the LFAM process, where fiber 
orientation could be continuously estimated and used for 
predictive simulations), in which fibre orientation is moni­
tored and predicted continuously based on microstructural 
imaging (e.g. via in-line X-ray or SEM inspection) [11]. As 
the generator is both physics-informed and parameter-con­
trolled, scenario testing is possible, allowing engineers to 
anticipate the microstructural effects of process parameters 
(e.g. deposition speed and nozzle orientation) without hav­
ing to physically print every variation.
The objective of this work is to develop a physics-
informed pipeline that combines experimental XRM 
imaging, synthetic image generation, and deep learning 
to automate the estimation of fiber orientation tensors in 
LFAM-manufactured composites [12]. Rather than relying 
solely on experimental data, which is costly and difficult to 
annotate, this approach enables full control over input fiber 
configurations and supports robust CNN training under con­
trolled, labeled conditions.
The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Sec­
tion  2 details the materials and experimental procedures, 
including the LFAM setup and X-ray microscopy protocol. 
Section 3 describes how X-ray microscopy (XRM) was used 
to extract high-resolution, virtually sliced 2D cross-sections 
from real ABS-GF20 samples. This enabled a ground truth 
analysis of fiber orientation and the validation of synthetic 
image generation. Section 4 presents the synthetic image 
generation methodology, quantitative parameters and data­
set characteristics. Finally, Section 5 concludes the work, 
summarises its contributions and proposes future research 
directions, including integrating physics-informed learning 
frameworks and extending the approach to other manufac­
turing techniques.
2  Materials and methods
2.1  Large Format Additive Manufacturing (LFAM) 
equipment
The experimental setup used for fabricating the specimen 
was based on a Super Discovery 3D printer. This LFAM 
system enables high-throughput material extrusion using 
thermoplastic pellets and offers significantly larger build 
volumes and deposition rates than conventional filament-
based 3D printers. The printing process is governed by a 
gantry-based CNC system that supports multi-axis motion 
and inclined layer deposition strategies.

The key specifications of the LFAM system are as fol­
lows: it features a build volume of 1300 × 2500 × 1000 mm 
and supports a material flow rate of up to 10 kg/h. The extru­
sion is performed through a 4 mm diameter nozzle, enabling 
layer heights ranging from 1.25 to 1.5  mm. The nozzle 
operates at temperatures between 230 and 250◦C, while the 
heated bed maintains a temperature of 90◦C. To ensure con­
sistent print quality and minimize moisture-related defects, 
a TDM 503–507 dehumidification system is employed, 
delivering an airflow of up to 80 m3/h at 80◦C for a dura­
tion of 4 hours. Figure 1 shows the additive manufacturing 
machine with the extrusion head attached.
2.2  Material specifications
The composite material used in this study is acrylonitrile 
butadiene styrene reinforced with 20% short glass fibers 
(ABS-GF20), specifically PolyCore™ ABS-5012 supplied 
by Polymaker. According to the manufacturer’s datasheet, 
the injection-molded ABS-GF20 material exhibits a density 
of 1.21 g/cm3 (ASTM D792) and a glass transition tempera­
ture (Tg) of 96 ◦C. The mechanical performance includes a 
Young’s modulus of 7343 ± 158 MPa, a tensile strength of 
90.6 ± 0.9 MPa, and an elongation at break of 2.3 ± 0.1%, all 
measured according to ASTM D638. ABS reinforced with 
20% short glass fibers (ABS-GF20) was chosen for the fol­
lowing reasons [14, 15]:
	
●
Industrial relevance in LFAM: ABS-GF20 is widely used 
due to its excellent balance between printability, stiff­
ness, and dimensional stability, making it a common ma­
terial in aerospace tooling and automotive prototyping.
	
●
Well-characterised behavior: The mechanical proper­
ties and processing conditions of ABS-GF20 have been 
extensively documented under both injection mould­
ing and LFAM conditions, facilitating comparison and 
validation.”
	
●
Microstructural contrast: The combination of polymer 
matrix and glass fibers produces high-contrast micro­
graphs under SEM and XRM, making this material ideal 
for image-based fibre orientation analysis.
However, when processed via LFAM, the material exhib­
its significantly different mechanical behavior due to layer-
wise deposition, fiber misalignment, and porosity. Tensile 
tests performed on printed specimens along the X (extru­
sion path) and Z (normal to layers) directions yielded the 
following: Young’s modulus of 3994 ± 159 MPa (X) and 
1943 ± 52 MPa (Z); tensile strengths of 74.6 ± 3.8 MPa (X) 
and 23.5 ± 0.7 MPa (Z); and elongations at break of 9.7% 
(X) and 5.9% (Z).

València using a ZEISS Xradia 620 Versa system with a

4  Synthetic fiber image generation 
methodology
A physics-informed synthetic image generator was devel­
oped based on morphological descriptors extracted from 
experimental X-ray microscopy (XRM) data to simulate 
microstructural images of short-fibre composites with 
analytically defined orientation tensors. These synthetic 
micrographs replicate the geometric and statistical features 
observed in LFAM-processed materials, providing a reli­
able ground truth for training convolutional neural networks 
(CNNs) in supervised regression tasks that aim to predict 
fibre orientation automatically.
Implemented in Python, this simulation framework can 
generate large, precisely labelled datasets that are tailored 
to the anisotropic microstructures that are characteristic of 
LFAM. Consequently, it facilitates scalable and reproduc­
ible AI-based workflows for the automated characterisation 
of materials. It is important to clarify that the simulation 
does not explicitly model melt viscosity, shear flow, or ther­
mal gradients. Instead, it captures the statistical outcomes of 
these physical effects by calibrating orientation and geomet­
ric distributions using descriptors extracted from XRM data­
sets. In this sense, the model is physics-informed through 
data rather than by solving governing equations. This allows 
it to realistically emulate fiber orientation patterns observed 
in LFAM without incurring the computational cost of full-
scale flow simulations.

Each fiber is modeled as an ellipse with a minor axis 
a = 6 ± 1 pixels and a major axis b ∈[30, 100], achieving 
aspect ratios from 5:1 to 15:1. Orientation angles ϕ follow a 
Gaussian distribution centered at 0◦ with σ = 5◦, resulting 
in ∼90% horizontal alignment. To model real-world vari­
ability, 10% of fibers are assigned random orientations in 
[−90◦, 90◦] to capture effects like print curvature. This local 
orientation dispersion is clearly visible in the SEM micro­
graphs shown in Fig. 5 (e.g., bottom-right), where curved 
or misaligned fibers appear near edges or irregular zones. 
Incorporating such heterogeneity makes the synthetic data­
set more representative of LFAM conditions, where simpler 
models often fail to reflect these microstructural fluctuations.
Overlap checks are strict: intersecting candidates are dis­
carded. This process continues until the fiber area covers 
20% of the image domain. The final images are saved as 
high-resolution PNG files (300 dpi) that resemble binarised 
SEM/XRM micrographs visually. The number of fibers 
per image (typically 750–800) and the area fraction target 
(20%) were determined by analysing cross-sectional slices 
obtained from X-ray microscopy (XRM) of LFAM-pro­
cessed ABS-GF20. These virtual slices revealed an average 
of 780 fiber cross-sections per image and a projected fiber 
area coverage ranging from 19% to 21%. These metrics 
were used to calibrate the synthetic image generator, ensur­
ing consistency with the real composite microstructure. 
Each synthetic image includes its ground truth orientation 
tensor A, either embedded in the file name or stored sepa­
rately. These labelled micrographs are used to train and vali­
date CNN models for predicting fiber orientation. Table 1 
summarises the parameters used.

and bi represent the semi-axes of the ellipses. These analyti­

The computation of the orientation tensor follows the 
formulation of Advani and Tucker [1], assuming that each 
ellipse corresponds to the planar cross-section of a straight 
cylindrical fiber. The method infers 3D orientation compo­
nents from 2D projections by relating the ellipse aspect ratio 
to the out-of-plane angle. While this provides a practical 
approximation, it does not account for effects such as fiber 
curvature or non-uniformity. Furthermore, only the diagonal 
terms of the tensor (Axx, Ayy, Azz) are estimated. To verify 
consistency, the same method was applied to experimental 
XRM images, yielding orientation tensor values with simi­
lar statistical properties to those generated synthetically.
Each ellipse represents the cross-section of a short glass 
fiber embedded in a polymer matrix. It is defined by its 
semi-axes (a, b), centroid coordinates (x, y) and in-plane ori­
entation angle ϕ. The ellipses are iteratively placed within a 
rectangular domain, typically sized 510 × 310 pixels, under 
strict non-overlap constraints. This process continues until 
the accumulated fiber area reaches a target volume fraction, 
which is typically set at 30% of the image area.
The orientation tensors (Axx, Ayy, Azz) are computed 
analytically for each image using the second-order orienta­
tion tensor formulation. To ensure spatial realism and pre­
vent overlaps, the algorithm uses spatial indexing via the 
STRtree structure from the Shapely library. Each candi­
date ellipse is checked against those that have already been 
placed; only non-intersecting ellipses are accepted. Vari­
ability is introduced into the geometry and orientation of the 
ellipses via random sampling.
	
●
The semi-major axis b is sampled from a uniform dis­
tribution in the interval [bmin, bmax] (e.g., 20.5 to 200).
	
●
The semi-minor axis a is drawn from a narrow range 
around a nominal value (e.g., 20 ± 0.5).
	
●
The in-plane orientation angle ϕ is sampled uniformly 
in [0◦, 90◦].
Once all the ellipses have been placed, the image is ren­
dered using matplotlib with white ellipses on a black 
background to simulate the contrast of an SEM/XRM. The 
images are saved in JPEG format, with the filenames encod­
ing the corresponding tensor components for traceability. 
Additional metadata, such as fiber count, area coverage and 
orientation statistics, is logged to aid dataset validation. The 
generation process supports batch mode and uses tqdm for 
progress tracking. On a standard workstation, generating an

Distribution-level realism  Beyond second-order tensors, 
the generator was benchmarked on low-order morphology: 
1.	 Fiber area fraction (p): the target coverage (∼20%) 
matched the XRM-derived range (19–21%), confirming 
calibration at the packing level.
2.	 Aspect ratio (b/a): synthetic samples reproduced the 
experimental spread of elongated sections, preserving 
the long-tail behaviour associated with oblique cuts of 
short fibres.
3.	 In-plane orientation (ϕ): histograms reflected the strong 
alignment induced by deposition, with controlled dis­
persion to emulate local misalignment observed near 
edges and curved toolpaths.
Where sample sizes allowed, two-sample tests (e.g., Kol­
mogorov–Smirnov on b/a and ϕ) were used as sanity checks 
for distributional similarity; full hypothesis-testing with 
power analysis is reserved for a larger experimental set.
Qualitative microstructural fidelity  SEM micrographs were 
used as a visual reference to verify heterogeneity patterns: 
mixed aligned/random fields, out-of-plane intersections (cir­
cular vs. elongated sections), and sparsely distributed voids. 
While porosity and fibre clustering are not explicitly modelled, 
controlled randomisation of ϕ and b/a reproduced the salient 
heterogeneity required for training robust CNN regressors.
Scope and limitations  The current validation is 2D and 
slice-based: it captures projected anisotropy but not full 3D 
continuity or curvature of fibres. As detailed at the end of 
Section 4, extending the generator to volumetric synthesis 
and 3D tensor estimation is a natural next step. In parallel, a 
broader statistical comparison against an expanded, consis­
tently annotated XRM dataset will strengthen the quantita­
tive bounds on ∆A and distributional distances.
Implication for learning-based pipelines  The combination 
of tensor-level checks, distributional realism and qualitative 
fidelity indicates that the synthetic dataset constitutes reli­
able ground truth for supervised training and benchmarking 
of CNN models in orientation regression. In practice, the 
explicit labels (Axx, Ayy, Azz) and controllable anisotropy 
enable balanced curricula and ablation studies (e.g., remov­
ing misalignment or narrowing the b/a spread) to probe 
model sensitivity in a traceable manner.

The synthetic generation methodology developed in this 
work provides full control over fiber orientation, vol­

4.1  Validation of the synthetic image generator
The validation strategy assessed whether the physics-
informed generator reproduces the key morphological 
and orientational statistics observed experimentally in 
LFAM-processed ABS-GF20. The analysis considered 
both (i) agreement of second-order orientation tensors 
(Axx, Ayy, Azz) computed from synthetic images and 
XRM slices, and (ii) similarity of geometric descriptors 
(area fraction, aspect ratio and in-plane angle distributions).
Tensor-level consistency  For each synthetic micrograph, 
the second-order orientation tensor A was computed analyti­
cally as described in Section 4. The same pipeline (ellipse 
fitting and tensor estimation) was applied to virtual slices 
extracted from XRM volumes (Section 3). As a basic physi­
cal check, all tensors satisfied tr(A) = 1 within numerical 
tolerance and A ⪰0. Qualitatively, synthetic tensors repro­
duced the anisotropic bias introduced by extrusion (i.e., Axx 
dominating in layers aligned with the X direction), consis­
tent with experimental observations. A compact discrepancy 
metric,
∆A = ∥A(syn) −A(exp)∥F ,
was used to summarise tensor-level differences across 
matched conditions (orientation bias, area fraction). This 
metric will enable expanded statistical reporting in future 
work as larger annotated XRM cohorts become available.

By removing human bias and significantly reducing 
the cost and time associated with experimental imaging, 
the proposed approach overcomes one of the key limita­
tions of deep learning-based material characterisation. The 
generated datasets have already been successfully applied 
in previous studies to train convolutional neural networks 
(CNNs) for orientation prediction, achieving mean angular 
errors below 1.5◦ and R2 values above 0.98 when evaluated 
on real microscopy images.
The methodology supports industrial implementation 
through its compatibility with digital twin frameworks 
and in-line quality control systems. It enables scalable sce­
nario testing and virtual optimisation, reducing the need for 
physical prototyping in applications where fiber orientation 
impacts mechanical performance and certification stan­
dards, such as in aerospace and automotive sectors.
Despite its advantages, the current approach is limited 
to 2D image generation and does not capture full 3D fiber 
curvature or continuity. Furthermore, it relies on statistical 
calibration from experimental data but does not incorporate 
explicit simulation of flow dynamics or thermal effects. No 
CNN model was implemented within the scope of this work; 
rather, the dataset is intended to support future machine 
learning applications. Additional statistical validation of the 
synthetic images against a broader set of experimental data 
remains an open task.
Future work will address these limitations by: (1) extend­
ing the image generator to 3D volumetric data; (2) inte­
grating physics-based flow simulations; (3) benchmarking 
CNNs trained on synthetic data with real annotated micro­
graphs; and (4) deploying the trained models for real-time 
orientation monitoring in industrial LFAM environments.

Furthermore, the use of synthetic data aligns with the 
growing trend of AI integration in materials science. It also 
supports digital twin frameworks, where fiber orientation 
prediction can be embedded into process simulations or 
real-time quality control. In summary, the methodology pre­
sented enables the systematic creation of robust, physically 
grounded datasets for training and validating AI models. 
This paves the way toward traceable and scalable mate­
rial characterisation workflows in fiber-reinforced additive 
manufacturing.
5  Conclusions
This work presents a physics-informed methodology for gen­
erating synthetic datasets tailored to fiber orientation analysis 
in composite materials manufactured by Large Format Addi­
tive Manufacturing (LFAM). A Python-based routine was 
developed to create microscopy-like images with controlled 
fiber orientation, aspect ratio, and area fraction, emulating 
the anisotropic microstructures typically observed in ABS-
GF20 composites. Each image is analytically labelled with 
its corresponding second-order orientation tensor, enabling 
supervised learning without the need for manual annotation. 
This routine is publicly available in an open-access reposi­
tory hosted on GitHub (​h​t​t​p​s​:​/​/​g​i​t​h​u​b​.​c​o​m​/​p​o​l​i​l​a​6​/​F​i​b​e​r​s).

Abstract: Large Format Additive Manufacturing (LFAM) enables the rapid production of composite components using short fiber- reinforced thermoplastics. This process offers high strength-to-weight ratios and efficient material deposition. However, the mechanical performance of printed parts is strongly dependent on fiber orientation. Reliable characterisation of ori­ entation remains challenging due to the limitations of manual microscopy analysis. It is further hindered by the scarcity of large, annotated datasets required for deep learning inference (i.e., the automatic prediction of fiber orientation from image data using trained neural networks). This study addresses this gap by proposing a physics-informed methodology for the synthetic generation of microscopy-like images that replicate the microstructure of LFAM-processed composites. The simulation pipeline, implemented in Python, creates large-scale datasets by generating non-overlapping ellipsoidal fiber distributions with known geometrical and statistical parameters. Each synthetic image is paired with an analytically computed orientation tensor. This enables the supervised training of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) without the need for manual annotation. The system allows full control over fiber orientation, aspect ratio, and area fraction. It is calibrated using real micrographs obtained via X-ray Microscopy (XRM). The resulting synthetic images closely repro­ duce the statistical features of real microstructures and provide robust ground truth for model training and validation. Overall, this scalable approach enables rapid dataset generation and facilitates the development of accurate AI models for automated orientation analysis. It also supports future applications in digital twin frameworks, in-line quality control, and material characterisation in LFAM.
